R-TOPIC.passage: A standard measure is usually treated as a technical matter, but its deeper effect was social. Before a measure was fixed, every trade needed an argument about the quantity itself. Such arguments were settled by local standing rather than by any shared rule. A trader moving between towns therefore carried not only goods but a running dispute about what a container actually held. Every such dispute had to be reopened in the next town he entered, and the cost of reopening it fell on the goods themselves. Once a single measure was fixed, that dispute disappeared, and the special skill of the people who had settled such disputes disappeared with it. Historians of trade often treat that skill as a casualty of progress, yet the exchange was never a simple loss. What replaced local judgement was a rule that strangers could check without trusting each other. Checking at a distance is exactly what allowed trade to reach beyond people one already knew.
choices: the condition under which early inspectors judged a container
differences among the containers that each town once held
reasons why trade among strangers stayed rare in every period
a fixed measure as the condition for dealing among strangers
methods by which a container was measured before the reform

R-FACT.passage: The first fixed measures were kept as physical objects in a public building. A bar of metal or a carved stone served as the object against which officials compared local containers. A copy of that object was then sent to each market town for daily use. The copies drifted a little every year, because metal wore down and stone chipped at the edges. Inspectors travelled between the towns to correct the drift in those copies. That work was slow, and the corrections were often disputed. A single worn copy could shift the price of grain across a whole region. Later the measure was tied to a natural constant rather than to any object. A wavelength of light does not wear down and needs no inspector. Any laboratory can reproduce the measure without a visit from an official. The metal bar became a museum piece rather than a working authority.

R-GIST.passage: Advice from an expert is often repeated as if it were a rule that holds everywhere. Yet every piece of expert advice was formed inside a particular set of conditions, and those conditions are rarely stated when the advice is passed on. A surgeon who insists on a long recovery period is speaking about the patients she has actually seen, most of whom were older than the person now reading her words. A coach who warns against early specialisation is describing the athletes who came through his own programme, not every child who picks up a racket. When the advice travels, the conditions stay behind, and what arrives is a confident sentence with its supports removed. The reader then applies it to a case the expert never examined and blames the expert when it fails. Advice is therefore worth as much as the description of the situation it came from, and no more.

R-CLAIM.passage: Schools record what students get right and almost nothing about what they got wrong on the way there. A test score marks the end of a process and hides every step that led to it. Teachers know that the useful part of learning happens in those hidden steps, yet the record keeps none of them. When a student cannot see her own wrong turns, she cannot tell a careless error from a real misunderstanding, and she repeats both. Schools should therefore ask students to keep a record of their own failed attempts alongside their results. The record need not be graded, and grading it would defeat the purpose. A workbook of dead ends is more informative than a page of correct answers. It only has to exist, so that a student can read her own past reasoning and see exactly where it bent.

R-MOOD.passage: Mina stood at the edge of the stage and looked at the rows of empty seats. In twenty minutes they would all be full. Her hands were cold and her mouth had gone dry. She checked the strings of her violin for the fourth time. Each note sounded thinner than the last one. She could hear her own heart in her ears. The hall smelled of dust and fresh varnish. Then the door at the back opened and her old teacher walked in. He gave her the small nod he always gave before a lesson. Mina felt her shoulders drop and her breath go slow. The seats were still empty, but they no longer looked like a wall. She lifted the bow and the first note came out warm and full.

R-IMPLY.passage: Every large organisation eventually produces a written document that describes how its work is supposed to proceed. The document is written by people whose job is to see the whole, which means their view is assembled from reports rather than from the work itself. Whatever reaches them has already been simplified twice: once by the person who did the work and once by the person who summarised it. The result is a description that is internally consistent and quietly wrong about the parts that resist tidy description. Those parts are exactly where the real difficulty of the work lives. When the document is then used to judge performance, the people doing the work are measured against a picture that was never taken from where they stand. They learn to produce the reports that the picture expects of them. In this way the map is drawn by the people who never walk the ground, and the ground gradually rearranges itself to resemble the map.
choices: those who design a system are shielded from the effort it takes to run it
records made for oversight come to replace the reality they were meant to record
organisations grow too large for any single document to describe them fully
workers resist documentation because it exposes the mistakes they have made
accurate description requires direct experience of the work being described

R-SUMMARY.passage: In a series of experiments, participants were asked to estimate how long a set of household tasks would take them. Half of them made their estimates in the room where the tasks would later be carried out; the other half made theirs in a neutral office. The estimates produced in the task room were substantially longer, and they were also substantially closer to the times the participants actually recorded. Interviews conducted afterwards suggested a straightforward explanation. Participants standing in the room mentioned obstacles that the office group never raised: a cupboard that sticks, a cord that has to be unplugged, a surface that must be cleared before anything else can begin. These small interruptions are invisible when a task is imagined as a single action. The physical setting did not make the participants more careful; it made the interruptions available to them. The difference persisted across participants of different ages and occupations. Estimating a task in the place where it will be done produced longer and closer predictions, because the setting made the (A) steps of the task visible rather than making the estimator more (B).

X-TITLE.passage: A weather forecast can be judged in two different ways, and the two rarely agree. The first way asks how often the forecast matches what the sky later does. The second way asks how often the forecast changes what a person actually decides to do. A forecast can score very well on the first measure and score nothing at all on the second measure. In a city where it rains on four days out of five, a forecast that predicts rain every single day will be right eighty percent of the time. That forecast is (a) accurate, and it is simultaneously useless, because nobody who reads it will behave differently on any day of the week. The forecast that earns its keep is the one that (b) separates the days on which a decision would actually change. Such a forecast will be (c) wrong more often, because the days it tries to separate are exactly the days that are genuinely ambiguous. Forecasters who are rewarded for accuracy therefore learn to predict the (d) exceptional, and forecasters who are rewarded for usefulness learn to accept a worse score. Most public forecasting is judged by accuracy, since accuracy is easily counted and usefulness is not. The result is a service that reports the obvious with great (e) precision and falls silent exactly where a reader most needs it to speak. A forecast is not a description of the future but an instrument for choosing, and an instrument is worth whatever it changes.
choices: The Long Road to Reliable Weather Prediction
Counting Rain: A Short History of Records
Why an Accurate Forecast Can Still Be Worthless
Precision and Trust: The Forecaster’s Dilemma
How Cities Learn to Live with Uncertain Skies

X-ORDER.passage: (A) Nora had spent the whole summer at her grandfather’s cottage beside the lake. On the last morning (a) she found him out on the dock with a wooden box in his weathered hands. Inside the box was a small brass compass, worn smooth around the edges from years of handling. "This one belonged to my own father," (b) he said quietly. "He carried it on every trip he ever took, and he never lost his way." Nora turned the compass over and watched the slender needle settle toward the distant shoreline. (c) She wanted to ask whether she could keep it, but the words simply would not emerge. (C) On the long drive home she kept thinking about the box on the dock. She thought about the needle that had settled so quickly. (d) She had said nothing at all, and the compass had gone back into the box before she left. Her mother noticed that she was quiet and asked her twice what was troubling her. Nora merely shook her head and stared out at the flat brown farmland. By the time they reached the city outskirts she had decided that the opportunity had vanished for good. (B) Two weeks later a small parcel arrived at the apartment with her name printed on the label. (e) She opened it at the kitchen table while her mother watched from the doorway. The compass lay inside on a folded square of soft grey flannel. Under the compass was a brief handwritten note in her grandfather’s careful handwriting. The note said that a compass is no use to anyone inside a box. It said that he had carried it long enough for one man. (D) Nora took the compass up to her room and positioned it on the windowsill above her desk. The needle swung once and then held steady. It pointed past the rooftops toward the distant water. She remembered the dock again, and about how she had not been able to ask. Then she wrote him a letter. She kept it deliberately short, because he had never liked lengthy ones. She told him exactly where the needle pointed from her window.

R-INSERT.passage: This is why such rules are almost always written after an accident rather than before one. Every safety rule in a workplace began as a description of something that had already gone wrong. ( ① ) Before the event, the hazard is one of a thousand hazards that could in principle materialise, and no organisation can afford to write a separate rule for each of them. ( ② ) After the event, the hazard is no longer one possibility among many; it is the thing that actually happened, and it now has a cost attached to it. ( ③ ) The rule that follows is therefore cheap to justify, because the accident has already paid for the argument. ( ④ ) A rule written before an accident has to compete for attention with every other imagined danger, and it usually loses the competition. ( ⑤ ) The pattern leaves an uncomfortable conclusion for anyone designing a system: the rules you have are a record of your failures, and the failures you have not yet had are the rules you do not have.

L-OPINION.passage: Dad, I abandoned my running plan again. That is the third failure this spring. I know. I exercise hard for a week and then I quit. Did you record anything about it? Not really. I simply ran. That is the part I would change. Recording it is the thing that keeps me going. Sounds like additional work. It takes one minute, and I put the date and the distance on a card. Perhaps I will try a card this week. Keep it simple, since one line a day is enough. I keep every card in a small box beside the front door. The box is the record.

L-MAIN.passage: Hello, everyone, and welcome back to our weekly practice session. Today I want to talk about how you change your form. Most of you try to fix three things in the same week. You raise your elbow, you shorten your step, and you breathe later. Then the whole stroke falls apart and you cannot tell why. The reason is simple enough once you see it. When two things change at once, the water gives you one answer. You cannot say which change produced it, so you guess wrongly. Change one thing and swim with it for a full week. Then the next change tells you something you can actually trust. That is the only honest way to learn a stroke.

So that comes to fifty altogether. It is. Do you need potting soil with that? Yes, one bag please. How much is it? A bag of potting soil costs twenty dollars. Actually, make it two small planters and two large ones instead. That changes the total order. And I am a registered member here. Members receive ten percent off the entire order. Are the large containers heavy? The large ones are heavy, but I can manage them. Do you want a carton for the small ones? Yes, one box is fine. The carton is free. Then here is my membership card.

L-REASON.passage: You look exhausted today. Did you stay up late again? Not this time. I was in bed by ten. Then why the gloomy face? I missed the morning bus. Was it your alarm clock? The alarm rang normally. I woke up on schedule. Did the bus arrive early again? No, it was perfectly on time. Then what happened? I had to return for my art folder. It was still lying on the kitchen table. And by then the bus was gone. Exactly. I waited twenty minutes for the following bus. You should place the folder beside the door tonight. The art folder was the only thing I forgot this morning. I ran all the way back to the kitchen for the folder. That is what I plan to do.

L-NOTMENTION.passage: Have you decided on the summer camp for your daughter? Almost. I am looking at the one by the river. Where is it exactly? It is in Pine Valley, about an hour north of here. How long does it run? Five days, from Monday to Friday. That is a good length. What does it cost? The fee is two hundred dollars for the week. Is food included in that? Lunch is, but not dinner. And what do the children actually do there? Mostly canoeing and simple map reading. My daughter would like the canoes. She already asked about the canoes twice. Is the river close to the camp? The camp is right beside the river. That is why the camp uses the canoes.

L-ANNOUNCE.passage: Attention, all visitors to the Harbour Wildlife Centre. The seal feeding session begins in fifteen minutes at the lower pool. Our keeper will explain how each animal is trained before the feeding starts. The session lasts about thirty minutes and there is no extra charge. Seating around the pool is limited to one hundred visitors. Please note that flash photography is not allowed near the water. Visitors with young children should use the ramp on the east side. The gift shop beside the exit will remain open until six. The lower pool is easy to find from the main gate. Just follow the signs for the lower pool. The keeper will be waiting by the pool. We hope you enjoy the rest of your day with us.

L-TABLE.passage: Here is the list of weekend cooking classes. Let us pick one. I can only do Saturday. That takes out the two on Sunday. Right. And I want to stay under fifty dollars. Then the last one is out. It is sixty. What about the length? Anything over three hours is too long for me. That leaves two of them. One is Italian and one is bread baking. I made bread all last winter. Then let us take the other one. How many people are in each class? The first two take twelve people. The others take eight people. That is fine for us. And where are the classes held? All of the classes are at the community kitchen. Good, I will sign us up tonight.

L-RESPONSE.passage: You have been quiet since the meeting ended. I keep going over what I said. About the schedule? Yes. I told them we could finish the report by Friday. And now you think you cannot. I think I can, but only if nothing else comes up. Something always comes up. That is what worries me. Why did you give them a date at all? Everyone was waiting and the room went silent. So you filled the silence. I filled the silence. And now the date is in the notes. You could send a short message tonight. Saying what? That the date holds if the survey data arrives on time. That is not backing out. It is naming the condition. I suppose the condition was always there. It was. You just did not say it out loud.
choices: Then let us cancel the meeting and start over.
Right, so put the condition in writing tonight.
You should never promise anything in a meeting.
I will ask them to move the report to Monday.
The survey data has nothing to do with the report.

L-SITUATION.passage: Daniel and Rosa are members of the same volunteer group at the community garden. Rosa has been leading the group for almost two years. Last week Rosa organised a plant sale that raised money for new tools. Daniel arrived late on the day of the sale and left before the clean-up. Rosa did not say anything about it at the time. Since the sale Daniel has noticed that Rosa gives him the smallest tasks. Daniel believes Rosa is still upset about the sale and has never told him. Daniel does not want the group to feel awkward for the rest of the season. Daniel decides to raise the sale with Rosa rather than wait for Rosa. In this situation, what would Daniel most likely say to Rosa?
choices: I think you should give the small tasks to someone else.
Thank you for organising the plant sale on your own.
I left early that day, and I would like to talk about it.
Could you tell the group that the sale went well?
You seem tired, so let me lead the meeting this week.

L-SET-TOPIC.passage: Good afternoon, class. Yesterday we talked about how animals find their way over long distances. Today I want to look at four animals that use very different instruments for the same navigation task. First, the monarch butterfly reads the position of the sun and corrects for the hour. Without that correction its path would bend further west every hour. Second, the loggerhead turtle senses the magnetic field of the earth and treats it as a map. A young turtle can hold a heading for weeks with nothing else to guide it. Third, the homing pigeon appears to use smell, building a rough map of smells carried on the wind. Fourth, the desert ant counts its own steps and keeps a running total of distance. When the ant turns for home it walks almost straight back to its nest. Four animals, four different instruments, and one navigation problem shared among them all. Each animal solves the same problem with a different instrument. Next week we will look at what happens when two instruments disagree.
choices: dangers that migrating animals face on long journeys
reasons why some animals travel farther than others
how scientists track animals across great distances
different natural tools animals use to find their way
changes in animal routes caused by a warming climate
